summary: Defines extensions to the sockets API for the Host Identity Protocol. They focus on public-key identifiers found through DNS and also provide ways to bind Host Identity Tags to locators manually. Applications can also support relaxed security models where communication need not use HIP. Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of calling a computer by its address, HIP calls it by a special name that proves who it is. This lets programs use those names through the usual network programming tools.

questions: what is a host identity tag
subtitle: Socket programming interface for using cryptographic identifiers instead of IP addresses.

tldr.problem: Applications using the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) need a way to call network functions based on cryptographic identifiers rather than IP addresses, but standard sockets APIs are built around addresses.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends the C sockets API with new functions and data structures to work with Host Identity Tags (HITs)—cryptographic hashes of public keys that serve as permanent identifiers—alongside traditional IP addresses.
tldr.outcome: HIP-aware applications can now resolve domain names to HITs, bind sockets to HITs, and discover peers using public-key-based authentication. The extensions remain experimental as HIP itself has not achieved widespread adoption.

facts.label: Identifier format
facts.value: ORCHID prefix (100-bit hash of public key)

today: RFC 6317 remains Experimental. While HIP was designed as a solution for improved Internet architecture and mobility, it has not seen widespread deployment. However, the API extensions provide a blueprint for how future cryptographic-identity-based systems might integrate with standard network programming interfaces.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) introduces a cryptographic namespace separate from locators, using Host Identity Tags (HITs) as endpoint identifiers. HITs are 100-bit hashes derived from public keys and formatted as IPv6 addresses with the ORCHID (Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers) prefix. However, standard socket programming expects IP addresses, making it awkward for applications to use HITs directly.

This RFC defines extensions to the POSIX sockets API (RFC 3493) to support HIP-aware applications. The extensions allow applications to resolve domain names to HITs via DNS, create sockets using the new AF_HIP address family, and manage both identifiers and locators explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: Network programming was built around computer addresses. HIP wants to use cryptographic IDs instead. This RFC shows programmers how to write applications that use those IDs just like the old address-based system.

sections.title: HIT-Based Addressing and Socket Structures
sections.content:
The RFC introduces a new socket address structure called sockaddr_hip, which contains a Host Identity Tag in the ship_hit field. HITs are 128-bit values, stored as IPv6 addresses, with an ORCHID prefix that distinguishes them from regular addresses. The structure also includes a port number, flags for future extensions, and a length field.

Applications can use wildcard addresses to accept any incoming HIT (HIP_HIT_ANY) or to accept both HIP and non-HIP flows (HIP_ENDPOINT_ANY). Different wildcard constants allow binding to public HITs only or anonymous HITs only, giving fine-grained control over communication modes.
sections.plainLanguage: A data structure now stores a HIT (cryptographic ID) plus a port number, just like the old structure stored an IP address and port. Wildcards let a program say 'I'll talk to anyone' or 'I'll only talk to verified users'.

sections.title: DNS Resolution and HIT Discovery
sections.content:
The standard getaddrinfo() function is extended to support AF_HIP as an address family. When an application sets ai_family to AF_HIP in the hints structure, the resolver queries DNS for HIP Resource Records (HIPRRs) that contain HITs and Host Identifiers, alongside traditional A and AAAA records for locators (IP addresses).

The resolver caches HIT-to-locator mappings with the HIP module, which manages multiple locators according to system policies. If no locator is available, the application can explicitly set locators using socket options defined in the multihoming extensions (RFC 6316). Applications can also operate without DNS, directly specifying HITs and locators if they already know them.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS lookup system is extended so when you ask 'who is alice@example.com?', it can return not just her IP addresses but also her cryptographic ID. Your computer remembers which ID goes with which addresses.

sections.title: Socket Operations and Multihoming
sections.content:
Once an application has HITs and locators, standard socket calls like connect(), bind(), and accept() work with sockaddr_hip structures. The getsockname() and getpeername() functions return the actual HITs after a connection is established, allowing applications to discover peer identities.

Applications can use socket options (defined in RFC 6316) to explicitly manage locators. For example, SHIM_LOCLIST_PEER sets the list of acceptable peer addresses, and SHIM_LOC_PEER_PREF selects a preferred locator. This supports both HIP opportunistic mode (communicating with unknown peer HITs) and explicit locator handling for multihoming scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs can now open connections using HITs like they use IP addresses. If a program switches network connections (like moving from WiFi to cellular), HIP keeps the same conversation going because it uses the cryptographic ID, not the IP address.

sections.title: Security Modes and Type Verification
sections.content:
The API supports both strict and relaxed security models. Applications can use HIP_HIT_ANY_* wildcards to bind to specific HIT types (public vs. anonymous), or HIP_ENDPOINT_ANY to accept both HIP and non-HIP data flows. New functions like sockaddr_is_srcaddr() and hip_is_hit() allow applications to verify the type of address returned and confirm whether a connection used HIP-based authentication.

The HIT_PREFERENCES socket option lets applications request specific source HIT types (public or anonymous). Applications using HIP_ENDPOINT_ANY should validate the type of the resulting connection to inform users whether their communication is authenticated or not. The RFC emphasizes that applications must be aware of these distinctions and choose security levels appropriately.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs can demand 'only talk to verified users' or 'talk to anyone, but tell me if they're verified'. New functions let them check what type of connection they actually got.
